text: In the twelfth month, the month of Adar, on the thirteenth day, when the king's command and decree were to be carried out—on the very day when the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them—the reverse took place: the Jews overpowered those who hated them.

The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to strike down those who sought their harm, and no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all the peoples.
All the officials of the provinces, the satraps, the governors, and the king's administrators supported the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.
For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread through all the provinces, for the man Mordecai kept growing greater and greater.

versions.text: For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame spread through all the provinces, since the man Mordecai grew ever more powerful.
versions.explanation: The idiom הוֹלֵךְ וְגָדוֹל denotes steadily increasing greatness; the repetition of 'great' echoes the opening of the verse and gives a stronger cadence for oral reading.

text: So the Jews struck down all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying, and they did as they pleased with those who hated them.
In the citadel of Susa the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men,
and they killed Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha,
Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha,
Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha—
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews. But they laid no hand on the plunder.
That same day the number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, "In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, along with the ten sons of Haman. What must they have done in the rest of the king's provinces! Now what is your petition? It shall be granted you. What more do you request? It shall be done."
Esther answered, "If it pleases the king, let the Jews in Susa be allowed to act tomorrow as well, according to today's decree, and let Haman's ten sons be hanged on the gallows."
The king ordered that it be done. The decree was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.
The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and killed three hundred men in Susa, but they laid no hand on the plunder.

The rest of the Jews throughout the king's provinces also gathered to defend their lives and gain relief from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they laid no hand on the plunder.
This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and on the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness.
But the Jews in Susa had gathered on the thirteenth and the fourteenth, and they rested on the fifteenth and made it a day of feasting and gladness.

This is why the Jews of the countryside, who live in the unwalled towns, keep the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of gladness and feasting, a holiday on which they send portions of food to one another.
Mordecai recorded these things and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far,
binding them to observe the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar year after year,

as the days on which the Jews gained relief from their enemies, and as the month in which their sorrow was turned into gladness and their mourning into a holiday. They were to keep them as days of feasting and gladness, sending portions of food to one another and gifts to the poor.
So the Jews took upon themselves what they had already begun to do and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast the pur—that is, the lot—to crush and destroy them.

But when Esther came before the king, he ordered in writing that the evil scheme Haman had devised against the Jews should fall back on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
Therefore these days are called Purim, after the name Pur. And so, because of everything written in this letter, and because of what they had seen and what had happened to them,

versions.text: Therefore these days are called Purim, after the word pur. And so, because of everything written in this letter, and because of what they had seen and what had happened to them,
versions.explanation: עַל־שֵׁם literally means 'after the name of'; 'word' obscures the wordplay with the term Pur introduced in verse 24.

versions.text: Therefore these days are called Purim, after the name Pur.
versions.explanation: The second half of the verse was dropped: עַל־כֵּן עַל־כָּל־דִּבְרֵי הָאִגֶּרֶת הַזֹּאת וּמָה־רָאוּ עַל־כָּכָה וּמָה הִגִּיעַ אֲלֵיהֶם ('and so, because of all the words of this letter, and what they had seen concerning this, and what had happened to them'). Without it the sentence no longer leads into verse 27, where the main clause ('the Jews established...') follows. The earlier revision's wording is restored while keeping the intentional change to 'after the name Pur.'

text: the Jews established and took upon themselves and their descendants and all who joined them that they would never fail to observe these two days as prescribed and at the appointed time, year after year.

These days are remembered and kept in every generation, in every family, in every province and every city, and these days of Purim will never cease among the Jews, nor will their memory die out among their descendants.

versions.text: These days were to be remembered and kept in every generation, in every family, in every province and every city, and these days of Purim were never to cease among the Jews, nor their memory die out among their descendants.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses active participles (נִזְכָּרִים וְנַעֲשִׂים) describing an ongoing observance, followed by imperfect verbs of assurance. Rendering it as past obligation ('were to be') weakens the enduring force of the statement and reads less naturally aloud.

text: Then Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with full authority to confirm this second letter about Purim.
Letters were sent to all the Jews in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus—words of peace and truth—

to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed times, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established for them, and just as they had taken upon themselves and upon their descendants the matter of their fasting and their lamentation.

versions.text: to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed times, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established for them, and just as they had established for themselves and their descendants, with the matters of fasting and lamentation.
versions.explanation: In Hebrew "דברי הצמות וזעקתם" is the direct object of "קיימו" (what they ordained), not a separate prepositional phrase; rendering it as "with the matters of" obscures the syntax. Also the possessive suffix in "וזעקתם" ("their lamentation") is dropped. The revised wording restores both and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: So Queen Esther's decree confirmed these matters of Purim, and it was written down in the record.

versions.text: So Esther's command confirmed these regulations about Purim, and it was written in the book.
versions.explanation: "דברי" is better rendered "matters" (matching the same word in verse 31) rather than the more legalistic "regulations"; "decree" better reflects "מאמר" as a royal word of authority, and "written down in the record" reads more naturally for oral delivery.
